title-group.article-title: Medial retropharyngeal nodal region sparing radiotherapy in nasopharyngeal carcinoma: five year analysis of open label, non-inferiority, multicentre, randomised phase 3 trial

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: To determine the pre-specified long term efficacy (survival and swallowing function) and safety of medial retropharyngeal lymph node (MRLN) region sparing radiotherapy for non-metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

sec.title: Design
sec.p: Pre-specified five year analysis of an open label, non-inferiority, multicentre, randomised phase 3 trial.

sec.title: Setting
sec.p: Three Chinese medical centres between 20 November 2017 and 3 December 2018.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: Adults (18-65 years) with untreated, non-keratinising, non-metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma without MRLN involvement.

sec.title: Interventions
sec.p: Eligible patients were randomised (1:1; block size of four) to MRLN sparing radiotherapy or standard radiotherapy. Randomisation was stratified by institution and treatment modality (radiotherapy alone, concurrent chemoradiotherapy, or induction chemotherapy plus radiotherapy or concurrent chemoradiotherapy).

sec.title: Main outcome measures
sec.p: The primary outcome was local relapse-free survival. The three year local relapse-free survival to assess the non-inferiority, with a margin of 8%, of MRLN sparing radiotherapy compared with standard radiotherapy has been reported previously. This updated report focuses on five year survival, toxicity, and quality of life. Additionally, a videofluoroscopic swallowing study and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measurements of pharyngeal contractors were used as objective measures of dysphagia

sec.title: Results
sec.p: This trial enrolled 285 patients in the MRLN sparing group and 283 patients in the standard group. At a median follow-up of 70 months, the MRLN sparing and standard groups had similar five year local relapse-free survival (89.2% (95% confidence interval (CI) 85% to 92%) versus 90.6% (87% to 94%); stratified hazard ratio 1.03 (95% CI 0.61 to 1.74); P=0.90) and overall survival (89.2% (85% to 93%) versus 90.3% (87% to 94%); stratified hazard ratio 1.06 (0.68 to 1.68); P=0.79). Updated safety profiles of the MRLN sparing group showed a lower rate of grade ≥1 dysphagia (45/206 (22%) v 70/216 (32%); P=0.01) and grade ≥2 dry mouth (33/206 (16%) v 55/216 (25%); P=0.02) and enhanced swallowing related quality of life (mean difference –11.9; P<0.001). Videofluoroscopy showed a lower prevalence of vallecular residue (49/66 (74%) v 62/62 (100%); P<0.001), pyriform sinus residue (32/66 (48%) v 45/62 (73%); P=0.01), coating of pharyngeal wall (7/66 (11%) v 17/62 (27%); P=0.01), pharyngeal transit time >1.0 s (1/66 (2%) v 7/62 (11%); P=0.03), and aspiration (8/66 (12%) v 18/62 (29%); P=0.03) in the MRLN sparing group. Additionally, MRI detectable late atrophy in the superior pharyngeal constrictor (mean thickness: 1.80 v 1.65 mm; P=0.005) and middle pharyngeal constrictor (2.34 v 2.15 mm; P=0.01) was less severe after MRLN sparing radiotherapy.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: MRLN sparing radiotherapy maintained uncompromised efficacy and better long term swallowing function by reducing radiation damage to pharyngeal contractors, supporting its use as a standard of care for non-metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

sec.title: Trial registration
sec.p: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03346109.
Accepted 2026 Feb 17; Collection date 2026.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The retropharyngeal lymph nodes represent the primary draining nodes in patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, with an initial metastasis rate as high as 70-80%.1 Traditionally, radiotherapy targets cover the entire retropharyngeal space, including both the medial retropharyngeal lymph nodes (MRLN) and lateral retropharyngeal lymph nodes regions.2 3 However, such radiotherapy volumes unavoidably expose pharyngeal constrictors, which are adjacent to the MRLN region and are recognised as dysphagia and aspiration related structures, to relatively high radiotherapy doses.4 5 This contributes to high rates of swallowing related complications, such as late dysphagia (35.4%) and aspiration pneumonia (12.0%), which seriously compromise the quality of life, and even threaten the life, of patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma.6 7 8

Recently, several magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) based studies have shown that retropharyngeal lymph node involvement primarily occurs in the lateral group, with a metastasis rate of less than 0.6% in the medial group.1 4 9 These findings suggested the potential feasibility of sparing the MRLN region. Additionally, the advent of intensity modulated radiation therapy has enabled the practice of sparing the MRLN region by spatially distinguishing between the medial and lateral groups and delivering different dose intensities to each group separately. However, during the early decades of clinical application of intensity modulated radiation therapy, the guideline recommended target delineation for nasopharyngeal carcinoma was still based on two dimensional era experience, which involved covering both the MRLN and lateral retropharyngeal lymph nodes regions.2 3 10 This practice no longer aligned with contemporary techniques.

Consequently, we conducted the first non-inferiority randomised phase 3 trial (NCT03346109) to compare the efficacy and safety of MRLN sparing radiotherapy versus standard radiotherapy (in which both the MRLN and lateral retropharyngeal lymph nodes regions were defined as clinical target volumes) in patients with non-metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma. So far, no other prospective studies have explored this question. At the primary analysis, MRLN sparing radiotherapy showed uncompromised three year local relapse-free survival and overall survival.11 The safety profile of MRLN sparing radiotherapy was favourable compared with standard radiotherapy, especially in terms of decreased radiation induced dysphagia and increased swallowing related quality of life.11 Nevertheless, the long term effect of MRLN sparing radiotherapy on survival outcomes and swallowing function remained unknown, and the rationale of decreasing dysphagia by using MRLN sparing radiotherapy needed to be explored. In this paper, we present updated efficacy and safety results at the protocol specified five years of follow-up. We report findings from objectively measured dysphagia to give a clear and comprehensive picture of dysfunction during the swallowing process in each stage and the corresponding radiological changes of anatomical structures to verify the principle of preserving swallowing function through MRLN sparing radiotherapy.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: This open label, non-inferiority, randomised, phase 3 trial was conducted at three major hospitals in China (Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Centre (Guangzhou), First People’s Hospital of Foshan (Foshan), and Wuzhou Red Cross Hospital (Wuzhou)). The trial design and methods have been reported previously.11 Briefly, eligible patients were aged 18-65 years with treatment naive, non-keratinising nasopharyngeal carcinoma (T1-4N0-3M0), and Karnofsky performance score >70. Patients were excluded if they had radiologically suspected or confirmed MRLN involvement, were planned for palliative care, had a previous malignancy, or had received treatment (chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or surgery) to the head and neck region.

The study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki and the International Conference on Harmonization Good Clinical Practice Guideline. The study protocol (web appendix 1) was approved by institutional ethics committees in each centre, and all patients provided written informed consent for participation.

sec.title: Randomisation and masking
sec.p: Patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to MRLN sparing radiotherapy or standard radiotherapy by use of a computer generated random list in a block size of four per stratum. Randomisation, stratified according to institution and treatment modality (radiotherapy alone versus concurrent chemoradiotherapy versus induction chemotherapy plus radiotherapy or concurrent chemoradiotherapy), was carried out centrally by the Clinical Trials Centre at Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center. The study was open label and allocation was unmasked to physicians and patients, although the central responsible radiologists and the statistician were masked.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: All patients received intensity modulated radiation therapy, with target delineation following the guidelines detailed in web appendix 2 (pages 3-15). Gross tumour volume included the primary tumour and the involved lymph nodes. Clinical target volume was divided into high risk and low risk according to incidence rates of tumour extension. The whole retropharyngeal space (extending from the base of the skull to the caudal border of the hyoid bone or caudal border of C3 as the lower limit) was included in the low risk clinical target volume for the standard group; only the LRLN region (contoured in the spaces medial to the carotid arteries) was included in the low risk clinical target volume for the MRLN sparing group, and the MRLN region (lying between the pharyngeal constrictors and the prevertebral fascia near the midline) was not intended to be targeted (appendix 2, pages 6-15). Standard-of-care chemotherapy (induction, concurrent, or both) was administered according to the extent of disease.12

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary outcome was local relapse-free survival, representing the time from randomisation to documented local recurrence in the primary site or in the RLN region or death from any cause. Secondary outcomes consisted of overall survival (time from randomisation to death due to any cause), distant metastasis-free survival (time from randomisation to documented distant metastasis or death due to any cause), regional relapse-free survival (time from randomisation to documented regional recurrence or death due to any cause), toxicity, and quality of life. Late toxicity was evaluated using the Radiation Therapy Oncology Group/European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) late radiation morbidity scoring schemes. EORTC Quality-of-Life Core 30 items (QLQ-C30) and Quality-of-Life Head and Neck 35 items (QLQ-H&N35) version 1.0 questionnaires were used to assess quality of life. The updated toxicity and quality of life data were collected over a window of 54-66 months.

Additionally, we did a videofluoroscopic swallowing study to objectively evaluate swallowing dysfunction, which was scored using the Videofluoroscopic Dysphagia Scale around five years after radiotherapy.13 14 15 Furthermore, we measured the thickness of the pharyngeal constrictors on the cross sectional images obtained from MRI at baseline and at three months, six months, nine months, one year, three years, and five years after radiotherapy. For the three year and five year time points, a window of six months was allowed. The methods for additional analyses are specified in appendix 2 (pages 16-21).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Details of the statistical analyses have been published previously.11 Overall, this trial was designed to test the non-inferiority of MRLN sparing radiotherapy versus standard radiotherapy in terms of three year local relapse-free survival, with a non-inferiority margin set as 8% (corresponding to a hazard ratio of 2.44). To achieve 80% power at a one sided type I error of 0.025, approximately 550 patients (275 per group) were needed.

We did updated efficacy analyses for the intention-to-treat population (including all randomised patients). We calculated local relapse-free survival, overall survival, distant metastasis-free survival, and regional relapse-free survival by using the Kaplan-Meier method, with hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals estimated using a stratified Cox proportional hazards model by centre and treatment modality. Patients whose first event was a distant or regional recurrence were censored for the local relapse-free survival analysis, and vice versa. We treated missing time-to-event data resulting from loss to follow-up as censored data on the basis of the last observation carried forward. We did subgroup analyses, multivariable analyses, and treatment effects analyses across subgroups for local relapse-free survival by using the Cox regression model.

We analysed late toxicity and quality of life in five year disease-free survivors. Patients who had both baseline and five year questionnaire data available were included in the updated quality of life evaluation. We summarised toxicities and videofluoroscopic abnormalities as frequency and severity; we compared differences by using Pearson’s χ2 test or Fisher’s exact test when appropriate. We transformed responses to questionnaires into standardised scores for comparison. We used a Mann-Whitney U test to compare differences between the treatment groups and adjusted them for the baseline values by using generalised estimating equations, with a 10 point difference in scores considered clinically meaningful. We used a Mann-Whitney U test for between group comparisons of pharyngeal constrictor thickness. We used SPSS software (version 25.0) and R (version 4.3.1) for all statistical analyses.

sec.title: Patient and public involvement
sec.p: At the time this study was designed, patient and public involvement in research was not yet a standard practice in China. Furthermore, regulatory restrictions on confidentiality of clinical data, combined with limited funding and the absence of formal training for patient and public involvement activities, precluded patient involvement in the initial study design, data analysis, or manuscript preparation. However, all participants were fully informed of the trial’s objectives and procedures during recruitment and contributed directly to quality of life assessments through questionnaire responses. We remain committed to sharing the study results with participants during clinical follow-ups and to ensuring broader dissemination through press releases, academic conferences, and social media.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Between 20 November 2017 and 3 December 2018, 599 patients were screened, of whom 31 were excluded and 568 were randomly assigned (intention-to-treat population) to MRLN sparing radiotherapy (n=285) and standard radiotherapy (n=283). The baseline characteristics were generally well balanced between the treatment groups (table 1). The data cut-off for this analysis was 25 July 2024, corresponding to 27 months of additional follow-up from the preliminary analysis. The median duration of follow-up was 70 (interquartile range 66-74) months in both treatment groups. Figure 1 summarises patient disposition at data cut-off. Overall, 545 (96.0%) of 568 patients completed regular follow-up until death or the latest scheduled assessment, and the remaining 23 (4.0%) patients with less than five years of follow-up data were lost (13 (5%) of 285 in the sparing group and 10 (4%) of 283 in the standard group).

sec.title: Efficacy outcomes
sec.p: At data cut-off, 43 (7.6%) of 568 patients presented with local recurrence, including 22 (8%) of 285 and 21 (7%) of 283 in the MRLN sparing and standard groups, respectively (appendix 2, page 35). Six patients had retropharyngeal lymph node recurrence, with no additional retropharyngeal lymph node recurrences since the primary analysis, and none occurred in the MRLN region (appendix 2, page 36). Details of disease progression and subsequent therapies are shown in appendix 2 (pages 35-37).

The estimated five year local relapse-free survival rates were 89.2% (95% confidence interval (CI) 85% to 92)% versus 90.6% (87% to 94%); stratified hazard ratio 1.03 (95% CI 0.61 to 1.74); P=0.90) (fig 2, top left; appendix 2, page 24) in the MRLN sparing and standard groups. The five year overall survival (89.2% (85% to 93%) versus 90.3% (87% to 94%); stratified hazard ratio 1.06 (0.68 to 1.68); P=0.79) (fig 2, top right; appendix 2, page 24), five year distant metastasis-free survival (84.8% (80% to 89)% versus 89.2% (85% to 93%); stratified hazard ratio 1.32 (0.84 to 2.09); P=0.23) (fig 2, bottom left; appendix 2, page 24), and five year regional relapse-free survival (93.7% (91% to 97%) versus 92.0% (89% to 95%); stratified hazard ratio 0.69 (0.36 to 1.30); P=0.25) (fig 2, bottom right; appendix 2, page 24) were also similar between the sparing and standard groups.

sec.p: Updated local relapse-free survival for pre-specified subgroups remained consistent among the subgroups (appendix 2, pages 25-28). In agreement with previous reports,11 we observed no differences in the updated local relapse-free survival between patients who underwent pre-treatment plasma Epstein-Barr virus DNA testing and those who did not (appendix 2, page 29) and between those who did or did not receive a pre-treatment positron emission tomography-computed tomography scan (appendix 2, page 29). In addition, updated local relapse-free survival was similar between treatment groups irrespective of a pre-treatment plasma Epstein-Barr virus DNA load of ≥2000 copies/mL or <2000 copies/mL (appendix 2, page 30) or the receipt or not of chemotherapy (appendix 2, page 31). Moreover, multivariable analysis for updated local relapse-free survival continued to show comparable prognosis of MRLN sparing radiotherapy to standard radiotherapy after adjustment for other covariates (appendix 2, page 38).

sec.title: Late toxicity for five year disease-free survivors
sec.p: In the updated safety analysis, we presented toxicity data in patients disease-free for more than five years (n=422), comprising 206 (72%) and 216 (76%) patients in the MRLN sparing and standard groups, respectively. The baseline characteristics of the five year disease-free survivors were balanced between the treatment groups (appendix 2, page 39). Consistent with the initial results, the sparing group showed a lower rate of grade ≥1 dysphagia than the standard group (45 (22%) v 70 (32%); P=0.01) (appendix 2, page 40). Interestingly, the only notable change was that the difference in dry mouth between the two groups shifted from being non-significant in the initial analysis to showing a lower rate of grade ≥2 dry mouth (33 (16%) v 55 (25%); P=0.02) in the sparing group in the current report.

sec.title: Quality of life outcomes for five year disease-free survivors
sec.p: As of the last follow-up, 256/422 (61%) five year disease-free survivors completed the EORTC QLQ-C30 questionnaire, with 130 (63%) of 206 and 126 (58%) of 216 in the sparing and standard groups, respectively. The EORTC QLQ-H&N35 questionnaire was completed by 284 (67%) five year disease-free survivors, comprising 147 (71%) and 137 (63%) in the two groups, respectively. The remaining patients refused to fill out the questionnaires or returned them incomplete. The baseline characteristics of the patients in the analysis for updated quality of life outcomes were balanced between the treatment groups (appendix 2, pages 41-42). In line with the initial analysis, the patients in the MRLN sparing group maintained statistically greater quality of life outcomes than those in the standard group, in terms of global health status (mean difference 5.8, 95% CI 2.5 to 9.1; P<0.001), role functioning (3.7, 1.3 to 6.0; P=0.002), social functioning (3.4, 0.2 to 6.6; P=0.04), fatigue (–5.3, –9.4 to –1.2; P=0.01), and swallowing (–11.9, –15.3 to –8.5; P<0.001) (appendix 2, pages 32, 43-44). Notably, the improvement in the swallowing domain continued to be clinically significant.

sec.title: Objectively measured dysphagia in videofluoroscopic swallowing study
sec.p: Among 422 disease-free survivors at five years, 128 (30%) patients (66 (32%) in the sparing group and 62 (29%) in the standard group) were available for the videofluoroscopic swallowing study. The reason for the lower availability of data was reported to be the reluctance of most patients to undergo invasive examination. The baseline characteristics between the treatment groups were similar for these patients (appendix 2, page 45). Overall, videofluoroscopic abnormalities mainly occurred in the pharyngeal phase of swallowing, with vallecular residues and pyriform sinus residues being the most common in both groups, which was considered a reflection of impaired swallowing efficiency. In comparison with the standard group, the sparing group had a lower prevalence of vallecular residue (49 (74%) v 62 (100%); P<0.001), pyriform sinus residue (32 (48%) v 45 (73%); P=0.01), coating of pharyngeal wall (7 (11%) v 17 (27%); P=0.01), pharyngeal transit time >1.0 s (1 (2%) v 7 (11%); P=0.03), and aspiration (8 (12%) v 18 (29%); P=0.03) (table 2). Thus, the mean Videofluoroscopic Dysphagia Scale score in the sparing group was markedly lower than that in the standard group (8.0 (standard deviation (SD) 6.8) v 15.6 (10.6); P<0.001) (table 2).

sec.title: Radiation induced MRI changes in pharyngeal constrictors
sec.p: After radiotherapy, the thickness of the pharyngeal constrictors showed the same trend of initial oedema, followed by a reduction in oedema, and ultimately atrophy, regardless of treatment group (appendix 2, pages 33-34). At three months after radiotherapy, the pharyngeal constrictors showed the most pronounced oedema. Subsequently, the oedema gradually decreased, and atrophy began to occur at around 12 months after radiotherapy (appendix 2, pages 33-34).

The mean thicknesses of the superior pharyngeal constrictor (2.06 (SD 0.49) v 2.07 (0.48) mm; P=0.92), middle pharyngeal constrictor (2.59 (0.65) v 2.61 (0.54) mm; P=0.12), and inferior pharyngeal constrictor (2.98 (0.67) v 3.02 (0.63) mm; P=0.26) were comparable between the sparing and standard groups at baseline (table 3). However, less oedema was seen at three and six months after radiotherapy of the superior pharyngeal constrictor (4.96 (0.77) v 5.09 (0.84) mm; P=0.04 and 3.88 (0.64) v 4.11 (0.75) mm; P=0.02) and middle pharyngeal constrictor (5.39 (0.87) v 5.56 (0.91) mm; P=0.03 and 4.37 (0.75) v 4.61 (0.82) mm; P=0.02) in the MRLN sparing group than in the standard group (table 3). Furthermore, the sparing group had less severe atrophy at three and five years after radiotherapy in the superior pharyngeal constrictor (1.97 (0.50) v 1.87 (0.46) mm; P=0.02 and 1.80 (0.46) v 1.65 (0.39) mm; P=0.005) and middle pharyngeal constrictor (2.48 (0.62) v 2.35 (0.52) mm; P=0.09 and 2.34 (0.56) v 2.15 (0.49) mm; P=0.01) (table 3).

sec.p: In addition, correlation analyses between dosimetry data and changes in pharyngeal constrictor thickness suggested that higher radiation doses were associated with more severe early oedema and late atrophy in the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors (all P<0.05; appendix 2, page 46). Dosimetry data for superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors also showed a significant correlation between higher radiation doses and more serious late dry mouth (all P<0.05; appendix 2, page 47), whereas dosimetry differences in varying degrees of acute dry mouth were not readily apparent (all P>0.05; appendix 2, page 47). Moreover, atrophy in the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors was significantly correlated with long term swallowing dysfunction, including observer rated dysphagia, videofluoroscopic swallowing study assessed pharyngeal impairments, and patient reported swallowing function (all P<0.05; appendix 2, page 48).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: With follow-up extended to five years, MRLN sparing radiotherapy continued to show comparable local control and survival outcomes in non-metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and these results remained stable in various subgroups. The updated data showed slighter radiation induced injuries, including MRI detectable early oedema and late atrophy in pharyngeal contractors, as well as the resulting lower prevalence of dysphagia and dry mouth, and enhanced quality of life outcomes in the sparing group, confirming the long term benefits of this de-intensification of radiotherapy to preserve swallowing function.

sec.title: Comparison with other studies
sec.p: In this trial, both standard radiotherapy and MRLN sparing radiotherapy provided satisfactory disease control, with five year local relapse-free survival, overall survival, distant metastasis-free survival, and regional relapse-free survival being similar to those in previous studies on non-metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma.16 17 Notably, no local recurrence was observed in the MRLN region, which echoed the extremely low incidences of MRLN involvement and recurrence in previous studies.1 4 9 18 The number of locoregional events increased only modestly compared with the three year report, whereas the number of deaths more than doubled since the primary analysis, likely reflecting the natural history of advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma and the impact of multiple salvage treatments aimed at prolonging survival.19 These potential delayed failures highlight the importance of long term survival monitoring and reporting. Together with the results of the preliminary report, the updated results highlighted the sustained efficacy and safety of MRLN sparing radiotherapy, supporting it as a standard of care for patients with non-metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Treatment of nasopharyngeal carcinoma has the potential to affect many critical components of the complete swallowing process20; therefore, a clinical need exists to identify those components that are positively affected by MRLN sparing radiotherapy. We applied an objective method using a videofluoroscopic swallowing study, which allows viewing and recording of the structures and dynamics of the swallowing process,21 22 23 to provide a visual understanding of the nature and characteristics of swallowing impairment. The findings of the videofluoroscopic swallowing study showed that the most common swallowing impairment occurred in the pharyngeal phase, characterised by pharyngeal stasis and aspiration; and the frequency and severity of these impairments were lower in the MRLN sparing group. The predominant cause of pharyngeal phase impairment is accepted to be functional deficits in the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors, because these muscles allow elevation of the larynx and contraction of the pharynx to generate bolus propulsion.5 20 24

Essentially, dysfunction of the pharyngeal constrictors is attributed to radiation induced pathophysiological changes in these muscles.25 26 To depict radiation induced changes in pharyngeal contractors and assess muscle pathology, MRI has been considered a useful tool because of its superior soft tissue contrast.27 28 Using MRI, we observed pronounced thickening of pharyngeal contractors caused by early oedema within six months after radiotherapy and a trend towards muscle thinning due to late atrophy at three to five years after radiotherapy, coinciding with the law of radiation induced pathophysiological changes in muscles.25 29 As expected, we also found less severe anatomical changes of these muscles (superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors) in the MRLN sparing group. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of long term observations of radiation induced anatomical changes in pharyngeal constrictors, although several studies have described thickening of swallowing structures in the early stage after radiotherapy,5 26 27 30 which supplements specific data on late swallowing disorders.

Anatomically, the MRLN region is located in the space between the prevertebral fascia and the pharyngeal constrictors near the midline. Sparing of this region not only led to a remarkable reduction in the volume and dose delivered to the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors,11 but also decreased the radiation exposure to the minor salivary glands and their associated secretory nerves, which are located within the submucosa of the pharyngeal wall.25 31 32 Late radiation induced injuries of minor salivary glands and nerve fibres reduced by sparing the MRLN region may account for the lower incidence of long term dry mouth. This speculation was further supported by the correlation observed between late dry mouth and dosimetry data. Notably, xerostomia is a well established predictor of patient reported swallowing dysfunction.33 On the basis of our new findings that diminished severity of early oedema and late development of atrophy in the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors were associated with reduced radiation doses, and that better functional preservation correlated with fewer anatomical changes of the pharyngeal constrictors, we concluded that volume or dose reduction in pharyngeal constrictors through sparing the MRLN region from the radiotherapy volumes was successfully converted to clinical benefits for swallowing function. Many studies reporting the dose related radiological changes in pharyngeal contractors,5 26 as well as their dose-volume-effect relations after radiotherapy,34 35 36 reinforce our conclusion that MRLN sparing radiotherapy reduces radiation induced dysphagia.

sec.title: Limitations of study
sec.p: Our study has certain limitations. Firstly, as noted in our initial report,11 these findings were derived primarily from Epstein-Barr virus associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma in endemic regions and may be extrapolated to Epstein-Barr virus associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma in non-endemic regions given their similar biology and failure patterns. However, their applicability to non-viral or human papilloma virus related nasopharyngeal carcinoma remains uncertain owing to the limited data on lymphatic drainage patterns in these subtypes. Secondly, this was an open label study, and toxicity data were primarily obtained through clinical enquiries, introducing some unavoidable subjective bias. However, we incorporated objective evidence from the videofluoroscopic swallowing study to strengthen and validate our findings. Thirdly, the assessment of dysphagia by the videofluoroscopic swallowing study was a post hoc exploratory analysis, and thus baseline data were lacking. Although baseline characteristics of the treatment groups who underwent a videofluoroscopic swallowing study were balanced, the number of patients was small, which may not rule out the potential for confounding and bias. Therefore, the subsequent findings are presented as a supplement to the main results, and prospective studies objectively evaluating dysphagia before and after treatment are warranted. Fourthly, whereas intensity modulated radiation therapy is photon based, proton therapy is a more advanced modality that exploits physical properties inherent to heavier particles to produce highly conformal depth-dose distributions, which might allow greater sparing of the MRLN region.37 However, the safety and the efficacy of MRLN sparing radiotherapy based on proton therapy need further verification in the future.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: MRLN sparing radiotherapy, through reducing early oedema and late atrophy of pharyngeal contractors, significantly decreased observer rated, patient reported, and objectively assessed dysphagia, without compromising efficacy. Our robust data provide a strong rationale supporting MRLN sparing radiotherapy as a valid option to treat non-metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

sec.title: What is already known on this topic

list-item.p: The primary analysis of this trial showed that medial retropharyngeal lymph node (MRLN) region sparing radiotherapy maintained uncompromised three year survival
It also improved swallowing function in patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma
The long term impact of MRLN sparing radiotherapy on survival and swallowing function remains uncertain
At five years, MRLN sparing radiotherapy significantly reduced observer rated, patient reported, and objectively assessed dysphagia, while maintaining uncompromised efficacy
Reducing the volume and dose delivered to pharyngeal constrictors diminished early oedema and late atrophy, with clinically meaningful improvements in swallowing function
These findings confirmed the long term functional benefits of this strategy and validated the principle of preserving swallowing function by sparing the MRLN region

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: The code used to analyse the data can be found in web appendix 3. The data underlying the findings in this paper are openly and publicly available and can be found at https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/vvnswtgdz8/1. If you encounter problems accessing the data, please contact the corresponding author. The raw data were also uploaded to the Research Data Deposit public platform (RDDA2026205661).
